specAnchors.text: understand how the brightness of a star at a standard distance can be represented using absolute magnitude

primer.text: Two brightnesses, one trap: apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks from Earth — luminosity and distance both interfere — while absolute magnitude compares every star as if placed at the same standard distance, 10 parsecs away. The scale runs back to front: brighter means lower.

modules.title: Luminosity and apparent magnitude
modules.opening: A star's luminosity is the total light energy it emits each second — its power output. What we see from Earth is the apparent magnitude, which depends on both the star's luminosity and its distance: more distant stars usually look fainter, and on the magnitude scale brighter means lower.
keyPoints: Luminosity counts all the light energy a star pours out each second — its power output.
Luminosity measures a star's brightness or power output.
Apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks to us here on Earth.
Apparent magnitude depends on the star's luminosity and its distance from Earth.
On the magnitude scale, brighter stars have lower magnitudes.

low.restatement: Luminosity = power emitted; apparent magnitude = what Earth sees, mixing power with distance.
low.analogy: Two streetlamps: a 2000-watt lamp far away can look as dim as a 100-watt lamp next to you.
low.examPointer: Remember the scale is back to front: brighter star, lower magnitude.

medium.restatement: Brightness as seen = luminosity diluted by distance; the magnitude number falls as the glow rises.
medium.analogy: Sprinkler reach: a powerful sprinkler douses you lightly from far away just like a weak one up close.
medium.examPointer: Two-factor questions need both factors named: luminosity and distance.

modules.title: Absolute magnitude
modules.opening: Astronomers level the playing field with absolute magnitude: how bright stars would appear if all were placed a common distance away — ten parsecs, roughly 32.6 light-years — some 3.04 × 10¹⁴ km.
keyPoints: Absolute magnitude measures how bright stars would appear at the same standard distance from Earth.
The standard distance is ten parsecs — about 32.6 light-years, roughly 3.04 × 10¹⁴ km.
Absolute magnitude removes the distance bias from brightness comparisons.
A bright far star and a dim near star can be compared fairly on the absolute scale.

low.restatement: Absolute magnitude = brightness at a fixed distance (10 pc), so the comparison is fair.
low.analogy: Standardised testing: move every contestant to the same starting line before judging speed.
low.examPointer: Quote the standard distance in parsecs — 10 parsecs — and the magnitude direction: bright = low.

medium.restatement: Distance is the confounder; the absolute scale deletes it by convention.
medium.analogy: Photo filters: apparent magnitude is the filtered photo, absolute magnitude is the unedited original.
medium.examPointer: The three equivalent standard distances (10 pc, 32.6 ly, 3.04 × 10¹⁴ km) are worth quoting once each.

glossary.definition: The light energy a star pours out each second — its power output.
How bright a star looks to us here on Earth.
Brightness as it would appear at the standard distance of 10 parsecs.
